question: What is the primary purpose of a nutritional assessment in a hospital?

options.A: To prescribe specific medications for pain
options.B: To evaluate a patient's nutritional status
options.C: To calculate daily hospital food expenses
options.D: To determine the patient's cooking skills

explanation: Nutritional assessment is specifically designed to measure a patient's nutritional health and identify any existing imbalances. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h1)

question: Why is early nutritional evaluation important for admitted patients?

options.A: It guarantees immediate discharge from the ward
options.B: It prevents complications before severe deficiencies develop
options.C: It eliminates the need for any laboratory investigations
options.D: It shortens the visiting hours for family members

explanation: Catching nutritional risks early allows nurses to intervene before minor deficits turn into major health setbacks. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h1)

question: Which components are typically included in a comprehensive nutritional assessment?

options.A: Surgical history, blood pressure, and mental status only
options.B: Medical, dietary, physical, and laboratory measurements
options.C: Housing conditions, income level, and religious beliefs
options.D: Occupation, shoe size, and family ancestry

explanation: A complete nutritional evaluation combines multiple data types to give an accurate picture of health. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h2)

question: How does nutritional assessment guide clinical nursing interventions?

options.A: By determining the correct dosage of intravenous antibiotics
options.B: By establishing the visiting schedule for relatives
options.C: By dictating the exact type of surgery a patient must undergo
options.D: By identifying specific imbalances that require dietary changes or supplements

explanation: Knowing what a patient lacks or has in excess helps the healthcare team plan targeted dietary therapy. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h2)

question: What does the letter 'B' stand for in the ABCD approach to nutritional assessment?
explanation: In the ABCD framework, B represents biochemical tests like blood and urine values. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h3)

question: A nurse checking a patient for swollen gums and muscle wasting is performing which part of the ABCD assessment?
explanation: Physical signs of nutrient deficiencies are observed during the clinical examination phase of the ABCD method. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h3)

question: Which complication is strongly linked to poor nutritional status in hospitalized patients?

options.D: Rapid healing of chronic pressure ulcers

explanation: Malnutrition weakens the immune system, making patients much more vulnerable to infections. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h4)

question: A nurse notes that a post-surgical patient has delayed wound healing and poor intake. What is the best immediate action?

options.A: Conduct a thorough nutritional assessment and report findings
options.B: Wait for the family to bring local food without checking
options.C: Restrict all fluid intake to prevent local swelling
options.D: Discharge the patient home immediately with no follow-up

explanation: Identifying nutritional gaps allows the nurse to collaborate with dietary services to improve wound healing. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h4)

question: What does the term malnutrition include?
explanation: Malnutrition is a broad term that covers any nutritional imbalance, whether it is a deficit or an excess. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h5)

question: Which patient group is generally at the highest risk for developing malnutrition in healthcare settings?

options.A: Athletes recovering from minor muscle sprains
options.B: Healthy volunteers participating in research trials
options.C: Elderly patients and those with chronic illnesses
options.D: Young adults visiting the clinic for routine check-ups

explanation: Older adults and chronically ill individuals often face decreased appetite, metabolic stress, and absorption issues. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h5)

question: When is nutritional screening usually performed for an admitted patient?

options.A: Upon admission to the healthcare facility
options.B: When the patient requests a special menu
options.C: Only on the day of hospital discharge
options.D: Two weeks after the patient goes home

explanation: Screening is done early during admission to catch potential nutritional problems right away. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h6)

question: How does nutritional screening differ from a full nutritional assessment?

options.A: Screening requires laboratory blood tests, while assessment does not
options.B: Screening takes several hours to complete for every single patient
options.C: Assessment is done by ward attendants, while screening is done by doctors
options.D: Screening is a rapid process to spot risk, while assessment is comprehensive

explanation: Screening acts as a quick filter, whereas a full assessment dives deep into the patient's nutritional data. [learn more](GNS227_U5_T001#GNS227_U5_T001_h6)
